title: QUICK TECHNIQUE: Deep Caries Treatment
html:
A deep carious lesion can make you pause, even when the patient says the tooth feels fine. The radiograph tells you there is very little room for error. The patient wants the tooth restored, preferably without a painful surprise afterward. So do I.

The challenge is deciding whether a restorative approach is appropriate, then giving the tooth the best opportunity to remain comfortable and functional. In my practice, Hemaseal & Cide (Advantage Dental, Inc) was part of that process, with the goal of improving the bond and minimizing postoperative sensitivity. Diagnosis, isolation, dentin handling, and the final bite deserve just as much attention.

The following case illustrates where this dentin-treatment step fits, from the initial evaluation to the final adjustment.

Evaluation and Preparation

The patient presented with extensive caries on teeth Nos. 20 and 30. Tooth No. 30 was treated first with a core and crown. The preoperative radiograph of No. 20 showed an extensive distal lesion (Figure 1).

When considering a restorative approach, I evaluate responses to hot, cold, and percussion, along with any spontaneous pain. The patient must understand that endodontic treatment may still become necessary.

A large lesion on an x-ray does not, by itself, settle the treatment decision. The pulpal and periapical findings matter. When those findings support a restorative approach, the question becomes whether we can restore the tooth while preserving its vitality. Avoiding endodontic treatment starts with choosing the case carefully from the outset.

After local anesthesia with 4% Septocaine (Septodont), I gained access with a No. 35 inverted cone bur in a high-speed handpiece. Once sufficient enamel had been removed, I switched to a No. 6 round bur at slow speed. A gentle touch is needed to feel your way through the lesion.

Caries-detecting liquid and a hand curette helped assess the remaining tooth structure. In this case, a pink area was visible through an extremely thin dentin wall (Figure 2). I call these “window exposures,” where the underlying blood vessels can be seen through the remaining dentin.

The remaining dentin represented a clinically important distinction here. An actual pulp exposure would require a separate assessment and treatment plan. Hemaseal & Cide was used to treat the dentin before bonding; it was not being used as a pulp-capping material.

Isolation and Dentin Treatment

The tooth was isolated with a rubber dam, and a Garrison Dental Solutions matrix system and ring were placed (Figure 3). I applied 40% phosphoric acid for 15 seconds, rinsed thoroughly, and removed excess water.

Next came Hemaseal & Cide, containing 4% chlorhexidine, applied with a microapplicator brush (Figure 4). I wicked away the excess by blotting the brush on gauze, leaving the preparation moist without puddling. That small distinction is easy to overlook when you are concentrating on how close you are to the pulp. This was the dentin-treatment step I used to disinfect and wet the bond zone before adhesive placement.

Hemaseal & Cide offered several benefits in a preparation this deep. The chlorhexidine provided antimicrobial action, while the HEMA-containing solution helped wet the dentin before bonding. Laboratory evaluations have also reported increased dentin bond strength and reduced microleakage. In my clinical experience, this step helped minimize postoperative sensitivity. Those benefits made it a useful part of the procedure when very little dentin separated the restoration from the pulp.

OptiBond Solo Plus (Kerr) was applied and cured (Figure 5). I then placed 2 thin layers of Estelite Flow Quick flowable composite (Tokuyama Dental America), using an explorer to eliminate bubbles before curing.

Completing the restoration

Estelite A2 composite (Tokuyama Dental America), was placed and packed. A Contact Pro light-curing aid (Practicon) was pressed firmly toward the distal contact during curing. After removing the aid, the remaining space was filled and cured.

The matrix, ring, and rubber dam were removed, and the occlusion was checked. An anesthetized patient cannot always assess the bite accurately. After I think it is perfect, I check 3 or 4 more times. Excess composite outside the restoration can fool you.

Figure 6 shows the completed restoration. The patient was instructed to call with any postoperative problems. A crown was recommended in the future.

The direct restoration was part of a staged approach. The crown recommendation addressed the tooth’s restorative needs, while its comfort and clinical findings guided reassessment. A tooth that remains asymptomatic still needs monitoring; comfort alone does not establish long-term pulpal health.

Clinical Perspective

I have performed this procedure many times, often when financial limitations influenced the patient’s choice. My favorable experience with Hemaseal & Cide led me to include it in the procedure, particularly in minimizing post-op sensitivity. I believe its ability to wet and disinfect the bond zone is an important contributor. Continued clinical and radiographic assessment is important, particularly when a lesion has come this close to the pulp. For me, treating the dentin is an essential part of restoring the tooth.

I always explained that endodontic treatment might still be needed. But a deep lesion did not automatically mean a root canal. In this case, the tooth remained comfortable and asymptomatic following restoration—the result we had hoped for. Giving a carefully selected tooth that opportunity was a satisfying outcome for both the patient and me.

Adapted from the author’s article in Dental Products Report, June 2007 and Dentistry Today, April 2019.
